Abstract
Osteocalcin regulates energy metabolism in an active
undercarboxylated/uncarboxylated form. However, its role on the development of non-
alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is still controversial. In the current study, we
investigated the causal relationship of circulating osteocalcin with NAFLD in two human
cohorts and studied the effect of uncarboxylated osteocalcin on liver lipid metabolism
through animal models. We analyzed the correlations of serum total/uncarboxylated
osteocalcin with liver steatosis/fibrosis in a liver biopsy cohort of 196 participants, and
the causal relationship between serum osteocalcin and the incidence/remission of
NAFLD in a prospective community cohort of 2055 subjects from Shanghai Changfeng
Study. Serum total osteocalcin was positively correlated with uncarboxylated
osteocalcin (r = 0.528, P < 0.001). Total and uncarboxylated osteocalcin quartiles were
inversely associated with liver steatosis, inflammation, ballooning and fibrosis grades in
both male and female participants (all P for trend < 0.05). After adjustment for
confounding glucose, lipid and bone metabolism parameters, the male and female
participants with lowest quartile of osteocalcin still had severer liver steatosis, with
multivariate-adjusted ORs of 7.25(1.07-49.30) and 4.44(1.01-19.41), respectively. In the
prospective community cohort, after a median of 4.2-year follow-up, the female but not
male participants with lowest quartile of osteocalcin at baseline had higher risk to
develop NAFLD (HR,1.90; 95%CI, 1.14-3.16), and lower chance to achieve NAFLD
remission (HR, 0.56; 95%CI, 0.31-1.00). In wild-type mice fed western diet, osteocalcin
treatment alleviated hepatic steatosis and reduced hepatic SREBP-1 and its

downstream proteins expression. In mice treated with osteocalcin for a short term,
hepatic SREBP-1 expression was decreased without changes of glucose level or insulin
sensitivity. When SREBP-1c was stably expressed in a human SREBP-1c transgenic
rat model, the reduction of lipogenesis induced by osteocalcin treatment was abolished.
In conclusion, circulating osteocalcin was inversely associated with NAFLD. Osteocalcin
reduces liver lipogenesis via decreasing SREBP-1c expression.
Keyword: osteocalcin, NAFLD, bone-liver interaction, SREBP-1c, hepatic de novo
lipogenesis

Introduction
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a disease characterized with excess
accumulation of fat in liver, which is closely associated with metabolic disorders such as
obesity, diabetes and dysregulation of de novo lipogenesis. At present, NAFLD affects
24% of the world population [1], and accounts for 4.79 per 1000 person-years of
cardiovascular disease-specific mortality and 0.77 per 1000 person-years of liver
specific mortality globally [2]. However, there are currently no approved pharmacologic
therapies for NAFLD/NASH [3]. Several medications targeting at multiple extrahepatic
tissues, such as thiazolidinediones [4], glucagon-like peptide 1 [5], and sodium-glucose
cotransporter-2 inhibitor [6], have shown promising therapeutic effects on NAFLD
through interaction between liver and multiple extrahepatic organs [7]. More effective
therapies were urgently needed with the hope to curb the rising trend of NAFLD and its
related diseases.
An interaction between bone and liver has long been proposed [8]. Evidence
showed that skeleton is not just a static organ that functions to provide support and
protection of human body, but also an important organ that secretes a series of
endocrines that regulate multiple metabolic process, such as adipogenesis, muscle
growth, energy balance and mineral ion homeostatis [9]. It has been recognized that
poor bone health and osteoporotic fractures are associated with NAFLD [10,11].
Several bone derived hormones were also reported to regulate liver function [8,12].
Among them, osteoblast-secreted osteocalcin might be one of the key players in
regulating energy metabolism in its active undercarboxylated/uncarboxylated form [13].

Osteocalcin is a 49-amino acid bone matrix noncollagen protein secreted by
osteoblasts. In 2007, Lee et al. suggested that osteocalcin deficient mice present
increased fat, hyperglycemia, insulin resistance and reduced insulin secretion [13].
However, two recent reports indicated that another strain of osteocalcin knock-out mice
did not show any metabolic disorder [14, 15]. In human studies, circulating osteocalcin
levels in both carboxylated and undercarboxylated forms were, in general, inversely
associated with risks of type 2 diabetes [16,17], central obesity [17], and metabolic
syndrome [18,19]. Several studies also indicate that low circulating osteocalcin is
associated with increased risk of cardiovascular diseases [20].
Recent studies indicated that circulating osteocalcin was negatively associated
with NAFLD [21,22,23,24]. Previous animal studies also showed that osteocalcin
treatment could improve histological hepatic steatosis [25,26]. However, the role of
osteocalcin on the development of NAFLD is still under controversy. Several studies
showed no change of circulating osteocalcin level in NAFLD patients [16,27,28,29]. All
of these studies were cross-sectional, which cannot guarantee the causal relationship
between serum osteocalcin and NAFLD as the prospective study we are describing in
this study. The mechanism of how osteocalcin affects the development of NAFLD is not
carefully studied. Two recent studies indicated that the beneficial effect of osteocalcin
on NAFLD might be secondary effect of either improved glucose metabolism or
ameliorated lipid absorption. However, osteocalcin receptor, G protein-coupled receptor
family C group 6-member A (GPRC6A), is highly expressed in liver [30,31]. It is highly
suspected that osteocalcin might directly regulate liver lipid homeostasis.

In this study, we analyzed the association of serum total and uncarboxylated
osteocalcin with liver steatosis/fibrosis in 196 patients who underwent liver biopsy and
the causal effect of osteocalcin on the development of NAFLD in 2055 voluntary
participants from a prospective community cohort. Furthermore, with animal models, we
investigated the potential direct effect of osteocalcin on liver de novo lipogenesis and
steatosis.
Materials and Methods
Study subjects
Our study analyzed two groups of population, including a liver biopsy cohort of 196
adults (92 men and 104 women) and a community prospective cohort of 2055 middle-
aged and elderly participants (857 men and 1198 women) from Shanghai Changfeng
Study.
For the liver biopsy cohort, a total of 196 adults who underwent liver biopsy for
suspected non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) were enrolled for analysis. The
inclusion and exclusion criteria were the same as our previous study [32]. Briefly, we
excluded the individuals with excessive alcohol intake (≥140 g per week for men or ≥70
g per week for women) [33], other liver diseases (such as hepatitis B or C, autoimmune
hepatitis, et al.) or use of hepatic protectants.
For the community prospective cohort, the participants were from Shanghai
Changfeng Study, which was a community-based prospective cohort study of multiple
metabolic diseases among middle-aged and elderly Chinese adults [34]. We enrolled
5626 participants from May 2010 to December 2012, and participants with viral hepatitis
B (n=163), hepatitis C (n=3), excessive alcohol consumption (n=645), without

ultrasound examination for liver fat content (LFC) (n=515) were excluded from the first-
round follow-up schedule. Moreover, 156 participants who died before the beginning of
first-round follow up were also excluded. The remaining 4144 participants were invited
to attend the first-round follow-up appointment, and 3262 (78.7%) participants
responded to the invitation. Among them, 2055 participants (857 men and 1198 women)
without the use of medications that might influence LFC (lipid-lowering medication,
hypoglycaemic medication or hepatoprotectants) were finally included for analysis[35].
After a median of 4.2-year follow-up, 296 of 1374 participants with normal liver fat at
baseline developed NAFLD and 259 of 681 participants with NAFLD at baseline
achieved imaging remission of NAFLD.
The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Zhongshan
Hospital, Fudan University (No. 2008-119 and B2013-132). Written informed consent
was obtained from each participant.
Histological examination of the liver tissue
Trained interventional sonographers performed the ultrasound-guided liver biopsy. The
hepatic histological changes were assessed by an experienced pathologist (XQ Hu)
using NAFLD activity score (NAS), which consists of liver steatosis (scale of 0-3),
lobular inflammation (scale of 0-3), hepatocellular ballooning (scale of 0-2) and fibrosis
(scale of 0-4). Steatosis was graded as S0 (0-5%), S1 (6-33%), S2 (34-66%), or S3 (67-
100%) [36].
Quantitative ultrasonography for LFC
An experienced ultrasonographer (WY He) carried out the hepatic ultrasound
examination using a GE LOGIQ P5 ultrasound machine (GE Healthcare, Milwaukee,

WI) with a 4-MHz abdominal probe. Before ultrasound quantification examination, a
tissue-mimicking phantom from Computerized Imaging Reference Systems, Inc (Model
057, CIRS, Norfolk, VA) was used to set the ultrasound machine. As detailed in our
previous work [37], the ultrasound image of the sagittal section of the liver/kidney and
the intercostal section of the right liver lobe were captured under the ultrasound
machine and analyzed using a NIH image software (ImageJ 1.41o, National Institutes of
Health, Bethesda, MD). Representative regions of interest (ROI) in the liver anterior
margin (depth 4–6 cm), liver posterior margin, and the liver parenchyma-right renal
cortex at the same depth were selected, and the echo intensity within the ROIs were
measured. We also measured the linear distance between the ROIs at the liver anterior
margin and posterior margin. The ultrasound hepatic/renal ratio and hepatic attenuation
rate were calculated using the following equations derived from the ultrasound
exponential attenuation law as follows:
Ultrasound hepatic/renal ratio = ultrasound echo intensity in the liver ROI/ ultrasound
echo intensity in the renal cortex ROI [37]
Ultrasound hepatic attenuation rate = (lnA
n - lnAf)/ (⊿d× f ) [38]
Where An and Af are average ultrasound echo intensity in the liver near-field and far-
field ROIs, respectively, and ⊿d is the distance between the above two ROIs. f
represented the frequency of the ultrasound detector.
Both ultrasound hepatic/renal ratio and hepatic attenuation rate were standardized
by the measured hepatic/renal ratio and hepatic attenuation rate of the tissue mimicking
phantom under the same machine setting condition and the LFC was then calculated
as: LFC (%) = 62.592×standardized ultrasound hepatic/renal

ratio+168.076×standardized ultrasound hepatic attenuation rate- 27.863 [37]. The LFC
cutoff for fatty liver by the ultrasound quantitative method was 9.15%, with a sensitivity
of 95.1% and specificity of 100%, according to our previous study [37].
Anthropometric and biochemical measurements
A past history of diabetes, medications, cigarette smoking, alcohol drinking and
menopausal status (women) was obtained from the medical history of the 196
participants who underwent liver biopsy and uniform questionnaires from the Shanghai
Changfeng Study. The body height and weight of the participants were measured with
no shoes or outer clothing, and we calculated body mass index (BMI) by dividing the
weight in kilograms by the square of the height in meters. We chose the midpoint
between the lowest rib and the iliac crest in a standing position and measured the waist
circumference (WC) using a soft tape. Resting blood pressure was measured using
electronic blood pressure monitors. After an overnight fast of at least 12 h, we collected
venous blood samples for biochemical tests under fasting condition, and then collected
blood samples again 2 hours after the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Fasting
plasma glucose (FPG), OGTT 2-h postload plasma glucose (PPG), serum alanine
transaminase (ALT), aspartate transaminase (AST), γ -glutamyltransferase (GGT),
creatine, cholesterol, triglycerides, and high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-c),
were measured using a HITACHI automated bioanalyzer (HITACHI 7600, Tokyo,
Japan). Low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-c) was calculated using the Friedewald
equation. Serum insulin, osteocalcin, 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D], β-isomerized
form carboxyl-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (β-CTx), procollagen type 1 N-
terminal propeptide (PINP) and parathyroid hormone (PTH) were measured using

electrochemiluminescence immunoassays. The osteocalcin was measured using a
Roche Elecsys N-MID Osteocalcin Kit (Cat# 12149133122, Roche Diagnostics,
Mannheim, Germany). The uncarboxylated osteocalcin was measured using a human
uncarboxylated osteocalcin ELISA Kit (Cat# 446707, Biolegend, San Diego, USA).
Homeostasis model assessment for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) was calculated as
fasting insulin (mU/L) x FPG (mmol/L) / 22.5. The NAFLD fibrosis score (NFS) was
calculated as: -1.675 + 0.037 x age (years) + 0.094 x BMI (kg/m
2) + 1.13 x impaired
fasting glycemia or diabetes (yes = 1, no = 0) + 0.99 x AST to ALT ratio - 0.013 x
platelet (109/L) - 0.66 x albumin (g/dL) [39]. Advanced liver fibrosis could be excluded if
NFS<-1.455, and confirmed if NFS>0.676. NFS between -1.455 and 0.676 was
considered “indeterminate” fibrosis [39].
Definition of incidence and remission of NAFLD
Participants who had normal liver fat at baseline but accumulated LFC by quantitative
ultrasonography to more than 9.15% during the follow-up were defined as patients with
incident NAFLD, while participants who had NAFLD at baseline, but reduced LFC by
quantitative ultrasonography to lower than 9.15% were defined as individuals with
remission of NAFLD, with reference to a previous publication [40].
Animal experiments
Detailed information can be found in the Supplemental Methods for animal experiments.
C57Bl/6J mice were purchased from Jackson Laboratory (Stock# 000664, Jackon
Laboratory, USA) and transgenic rats expressing epitope-tagged full-length human
SREBP-1c in liver under control of the constitutive apolipoprotein E promoter/enhancer
were constructed previously [41]. The animals were housed in a 12 hour light/ 12 hour

dark cycle colony with free access to food and water. All experiments shown were
performed with 12-14 week-old mice or rats. For short-term treatment experiment,
uncarboxylated osteocalcin (Osteocalcin-189H, Creative BioMart, USA) or vehicle
control was injected through peritoneal at the dose of 30 ng/g body weight for 7 days in
chow-diet feeding male and female mice or human SREBP-1c transgenic rats before
any analysis was performed. For long-term treatment experiment, uncarboxylated
osteocalcin or vehicle control was injected through peritoneal at the dose of 30 ng/g
body weight for 3 weeks in western-diet (Cat# D12079B, Research Diets, USA) feeding
mice. All animal experiments were performed with the approval of the Institutional
Animal Care and Research Advisory Committee at the University of Texas
Southwestern Medical Center.
After osteocalcin treatment, the study animals were sacrificed and the livers and
bloods were collected. Blood glucose, plasma triglycerides, cholesterol, insulin, liver
triglycerides and cholesterol levels and the expression of genes and proteins involving
liver lipid metabolism were measured. Glucose tolerance test (GTT) and insulin
tolerance test (ITT) were also performed in wild-type mice after 7-day injection of
osteocalcin.
Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses of the population studies were performed using SPSS version
18.0 software. The normally distributed variables are presented as the means ± SD and
the skewed variables are presented as the median with the interquartile range (25-
75%). The male and female participants were analyzed separately, and were divided
into gender-specific quartile groups of serum osteocalcin or uncarboxylated osteocalcin

before analysis. We compared the continuous parameters using one-way analysis of
variance (ANOVA) or Kruskal-Wallis H test, and categorical variables using the chi-
squared test. The quantitative correlations of serum total osteocalcin with
uncarboxylated osteocalcin, liver fat content and liver enzymes were evaluated using
Spearman correlation analysis. Linear-by-linear association chi-squared tests and
multivariate ordinal regression analyses were used to investigate the associations of
quartiles of circulating osteocalcin with liver histological steatosis, ballooning and
fibrosis grades. Test of parallel lines showed that the slope coefficients in the ordinal
regression models were the same across response categories. Multivariate Cox
proportional hazard regression models were used to calculate hazard ratios (HRs) and
95% confidence intervals for the incidence and remission of NAFLD in relation to the
baseline quartiles of circulating osteocalcin. Variables adjusted in the above statistical
regression models included age, BMI, cigarette smoking, alcohol drinking, menopausal
status in women, presence of diabetes, serum FPG, cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL-c,
LDL-c, 25(OH)D and PTH. Data of the animal studies were analyzed using student’s t
test. P-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant for all analyses.
Results
Serum osteocalcin level was negatively correlated with liver histological steatosis
and fibrosis.
A total of 196 adults with an average age of 47.7 years old and BMI of 27.1 kg/m2 were
enrolled in the liver biopsy cohort. Based on serum total or uncarboxylated osteocalcin
levels, the 196 participants from the liver biopsy cohort were grouped according to the
gender-specific quartiles of serum osteocalcin (uncarboxylated osteocalcin): Q1,

osteocalcin < 12.1 ng/ml for men and < 12.5 ng/ml for women (uncarboxylated
osteocalcin < 4.67 ng/ml for men and < 4.13 ng/ml for women); Q2, osteocalcin ≥ 12.1
ng/ml and <16.4 ng/ml for men and ≥ 12.5 ng/ml and <15.7 ng/ml for women
(uncarboxylated osteocalcin ≥ 4.67 ng/ml and < 6.63 ng/ml for men and ≥ 4.13 ng/ml
and < 6.92 ng/ml for women); Q3, osteocalcin ≥ 16.4 ng/ml and < 21.5 ng/ml for men
and ≥ 15.7 ng/ml and < 19.1 ng/ml for women (uncarboxylated osteocalcin ≥ 6.63 ng/ml
and < 11.93 ng/ml for men and ≥ 6.92 ng/ml and < 11.41 ng/ml for women); Q4,
osteocalcin ≥ 21.5 ng/ml for men and ≥ 19.1 ng/ml for women (uncarboxylated
osteocalcin ≥ 11.93 ng/ml for men and ≥ 11.41 ng/ml for women). The baseline
characteristics of these subjects are shown in Table 1. Higher serum total and
uncarboxylated osteocalcin quartiles were associated with lower BMI, insulin resistance
level measured by HOMR-IR and proportion of metabolic syndrome. Moreover, FPG,
PPG, serum triglycerides, diastolic blood pressue and proportion of diabetes were
signficantly lower in participants with higher quartiles of serum total osteocalcin (all P <
0.05). Additionally, serum total and uncarboxylated osteocalcin was also highly
correlated with serum 𝛽𝛽-CTx and PINP (Table 1).
We further analyzed the relationship of circulating total and uncarboxylated
osteocalcin with liver histological steatosis, ballooning degeneration, lobular
inflammation and fibrosis grades. Higher serum total osteocalcin quartiles were
correlated with milder liver steatosis in both male (P for trend = 0.037) and female
participants (P for trend = 0.008) (Figure 1A&B), and the association between the serum
uncarboxylated osteocalcain, the active form of osteocalcin, and liver steatosis grades
showed similar results in both male (P for trend = 0.005) and female participants (P for

trend = 0.006) (Figure 1C&D). Representative liver hematoxylin and eosin (H.E.) and
reticulin stained sections of participants with highest (Q4) and lowest (Q1) quartile of
osteocalcin were shown in Figure 1E, and liver biopsies from patients with high level of
serum osteocalcin showed dramatically reduced liver lipid droplet and improved liver
fibrosis. Total osteocalcin was highly positively correlated with uncarboxylated
osteocalcin (r=0.528, P<0.001) (Figure 1F). In addition, both serum total and
uncarboxylated osteocalcin levels were inversely correlated the histological
hepatocellular ballooning, lobular inflammation and fibrosis grades in male and female
participants (all P for trend <0.05) (Figure S1A-F). In comparison, other bone turnover
markers, such as β-CTx and PINP, had no significant association with liver steatosis
grades (Figure S2).
Comparing to the subjects in the osteocalcin Q4 group, the odds ratios (ORs) for
severer liver steatosis in the osteocalcin Q1, Q2 and Q3 groups were 4.58 (1.43-14.64),
2.87 (0.91-9.11) and 4.60 (1.44-14.72) in the male participants (Table 2), and 4.74(1.70-
13.29), 2.11(0.78-5.70) and 2.26(0.84-6.13) in the female participants (Table 3),
respectively. After gradual adjustment for age, BMI, cigarette smoking, alcohol drinking,
menopausal status in women, presence of diabetes and confounding glucose, lipid and
bone metabolism parameters, the negative correlation between serum osteocalcin and
liver steatosis grade was still significant with the multivariate-adjusted ORs of 7.25(1.07-
49.30) and 4.44(1.01-19.41) in male and female osteocalcin Q1 groups, compared with
the Q4 participants (Table 2&3). For the association between uncarboxylated
osteocalcin and liver steatosis, the unadjusted ORs in the Q1, Q2 and Q3 groups of
uncarboxylated osteocalcin were 5.09(1.60-16.14), 2.74(0.87-8.60) and 2.72(0.87-8.52)

in the male participants (Table 2), and 5.16(1.83-14.51), 2.72(0.99-7.43) and 3.75(1.36-
10.38) in the female participants (Table 3), respectively, comparing to Q4 participants.
After multiple adjustment, the participants with lowest quartile of uncarboxylated
osteocalcin still had a higher liver steatosis grades in the female participants (OR, 3.96;
95%CI, 1.09-14.30) (Table 3), and a trend of higher liver steatosis grades in the male
participants (OR, 5.10; 95%CI, 0.97-26.82) (Table 2). Since serum uncarboxylated form
of osteocalcin was highly correlated with total osteocalcin, and did not show stronger
correlation with NAFLD in comparison with total osteocalcin, only serum total
osteocalcin was measured in the rest of the studies.
Serum osteocalcin level was negatively correlated with liver fat content in large-
scale community population.
To further investigate the association between serum osteocalcin and NAFLD in general
community population, the quantitative correlation between serum osteocalcin and liver
fat content was analyzed in 2055 middle-aged and elderly community adults aged over
45 years from Shanghai Changfeng Study. All participants were divided into groups
according to the gender-specific quartiles of serum osteocalcin: Q1, osteocalcin < 13.5
ng/ml for men and < 16.5 ng/ml for women; Q2, osteocalcin ≥ 13.5 ng/ml and <16.7
ng/ml for men and ≥ 16.5 ng/ml and <21.2 ng/ml for women; Q3, osteocalcin ≥ 16.7
ng/ml and < 20.6 ng/ml for men and ≥ 21.2 ng/ml and < 26.0 ng/ml for women; Q4,
osteocalcin ≥ 20.6 ng/ml for men and ≥ 26.0 ng/ml for women, because osteocalcin
levels are increased in postmenopausal women and significantly higher than men [42].
As shown in Table 4, the proportions of NAFLD in the Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q4 groups of
osteocalcin were 37.4%, 36.0%, 27.4% and 29.4% (P for trend = 0.024) in the male

participants, and 38.1%, 35.3%, 33.8% and 26.3% (P for trend = 0.002) in the female
participants, respectively. The proportions of advanced liver fibrosis, determined by liver
ultrasonography and NAFLD fibrosis score, were significantly higher in the female (P for
trend = 0.007) but not male participants (P for trend = 0.075) with lower osteocalcin
quartiles. The prevalence of diabetes and metabolic syndrome was also higher in
participants with lower quartiles of serum osteocalcin in both male and female
participants, accompanied with higher BMI, waist circumference, hip circumference,
FPG, PPG, HbA1c, HOMA-IR, serum triglycerides, ALT, and lower serum HDL-c and
PTH (all P < 0.05).
Quantitatively, participants with NAFLD had lower serum osteocalcin than those
without NAFLD (Figure 2A). Baseline serum osteocalcin was negatively associated with
LFC (Male: r = -0.087, P = 0.019; Female: r = -0.129, P <0.001), serum ALT (Male: r = -
0.143, P <0.001; Female: r = -0.084, P = 0.006) and GGT (Male: r = -0.088, P = 0.017;
Female: r = -0.086, P = 0.005) in both male and female participants (Figure 2C-F).
Serum osteocalcin level predicted the incidence and remission rate of NAFLD in
female but not male community population.
To explore the causal relationship between serum osteocalcin and the development and
remission of NAFLD in humans, we finished follow-up examinations for the 2055
participants from Shanghai Changfeng Study. After a median of 4.2 years of follow-up,
an inverse correlation between changes in LFC and baseline osteocalcin quartiles was
found in female (P for trend =0.026) but not male (P for trend = 0.202) participants
(Figure 3A&B). The baseline osteocalcin levels had no significant association with the
incident and remission rates of NAFLD in the male participants (Figure 3C&E).

However, in female participants, the incidence rates of NAFLD were 30.6%, 23.6%,
22.2% and 13.6% in the Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q4 groups of osteocalcin, respectively (P for
trend < 0.001) (Figure 3D). After adjustment for multiple confounding parameters, the
risk of incident NAFLD was significantly higher in participants from Q1(HR, 1.90; 95%CI,
1.14 - 3.16) and Q3 (HR, 1.69; 95%CI, 1.04 - 2.74) group of osteocalcin, comparing to
Q4 participants (Table 5). Consistently, the remission rates of NAFLD increased from
26.3% to 44.9% with increasing serum osteocalcin (P for trend = 0.033) (Figure 3F).
Cox proportional hazard regression analysis showed that participants within the Q1 and
Q2 group of osteocalcin had lower remission rate of NAFLD than participants within
highest quartile of osteocalcin (Q4) after multiple adjustment, and the adjusted HRs
were 0.56(0.31-1.00) and 0.61(0.38-0.99), respectively (Table 6).
Osteocalcin reduces hepatic lipogenesis via inhibition of SREBP-1c expression.
Previous animal studies showed that osteocalcin treatment improved hepatic steatosis
[25,26]. However, in these studies, the beneficial effects of osteocalcin on liver steatosis
were achieved after a prolonged period of treatment with osteocalcin, which might
induce multiple change of metabolic symptom and masked the direct effect of
osteocalcin on liver lipid metabolism [25,26]. To delineate the mechanism of how
osteocalcin can improve liver steatosis, in the current study, mice were treated with
osteocalcin for only 7 days. The osteocalcin treated mice showed similar body weight,
liver weight, blood glucose and insulin levels. Liver cholesterol and triglycerides level
were not changed due to the short period of treatment. However, plasma triglycerides
but not cholesterol level was significantly reduced after 7 days of osteocalcin treatment
(Figure 4A-H). Intriguingly, liver gene expression by quantitative real time PCR showed

that SREBP-1c and the downstream lipogenic gene expression, such as ACC-1, FAS,
were reduced. PNPLA3, an important gene that increased in most NAFLD patients and
regulated by SREBP-1, was also significantly reduced (Figure 4I). The mRNA results
were confirmed by immunoblotting data. Both SREBP-1 precursor (P) and processed
nuclear (N) form and its downstream ACC and FAS proteins were decreased in the
osteocalcin treated group. In contrast to gene expression, SREBP-2 protein was also
reduced by osteocalcin treatment (Figure 4J).
To evaluate whether the change of SREBP-1c expression was induced by
alteration of insulin signaling, glucose tolerance test and insulin tolerance test were
performed after 7-day treatment of osteocalcin. Mice response similar to glucose or
insulin challenge in control and osteocalcin treated groups (Figure 4K&L). The 7-day
exogenous osteocalcin intervention was repeated in female mice showing similar
reduction in plasma triglycerides and hepatic de novo lipogenesis as the male mice
(Figure S3).
The short-term osteocalcin treatment on chow fed mice showed reduced hepatic
lipogenesis gene and protein expression without alteration of glucose and insulin levels.
However, liver lipids were not reduced by osteocalcin treatment due to the low liver lipid
content in chow fed mice and relatively short-term treatment. To study the effect of
osteocalcin on hepatic steatosis, another set of mice fed western diet were treated with
osteocalcin for 3 weeks. The osteocalcin treated mice showed reduced liver weight and
hepatic triglycerides and cholesterol concentration, despite of similar body weight after
3-week intervention (Figure 5A-D). The blood glucose and plasma triglycerides were
also significantly decreased (Figure 5E&G). Western blotting showed a reduction in

hepatic SREBP-1 and SREBP-2 precursor and nuclear form, as well as downstream
ACC and FAS proteins (Figure 5I), which was consistent with the results of 7-day
treatment of exogenous osteocalcin treatment.
To further explore the important role of osteocalcin in mediating hepatic SREBP-
1c expression, transgenic rats overexpressing epitope-tagged full-length human
SREBP-1c (hSREBP-1c) in liver were used. In this transgenic rat model, the hSREBP-
1c driven by a human apoE promotor/enhancer cassette is constantly expressed [41].
The plasma cholesterol and triglycerides, blood glucose and plasma insulin were similar
between control and osteocalcin treated group after 7-day treatment (Figure 6A-D). As
expected the transgenic human SREBP-1c (hSREBP-1c) gene was not affected after 7
days of osteocalcin treatment, even though the endogenous rSREBP-1c was slightly
reduced. Consequently, the SREBP-1c downstream lipogenic genes were not changed
in the treatment group (Figure 6E). Western blotting confirmed that SREBP-1 precursor
and nuclear form were not reduced in protein level by osteocalcin treatment (Figure 6F).
Discussion
Osteoblast-secreted osteocalcin has shown multiple metabolic benefits, but the
relationship between osteocalcin and NAFLD is still controversial. One possible
explanation for the controversy is the cross-sectional design and the use of ultrasound
as diagnostic method for NAFLD in most of previous studies, which limited the
evaluation of causal relationship and the accuracy of NAFLD diagnosis as well as the
possibility of liver fibrosis evaluation. Here, in a liver biopsy cohort of 196 participants,
we found that circulating osteocalcin levels were inversely associated with liver
histological steatosis, inflammation, ballooning and fibrosis grades. In addition, with a

median of 4.2-year follow-up, we proposed that serum osteocalcin level could predict
NAFLD incidence and remission independent of insulin resistance level and other
metabolic parameters in female participants. To the best of our knowledge, this is the
first prospective cohort study to show the reversal causal effect of osteocalcin on the
development of NAFLD. Further study in animal models showed that osteocalcin could
reduce hepatic lipogenesis and triglycerides accumulation in a SREBP-1c dependent
manner, and this effect was independent of the changes of glucose and insulin levels.
Most human studies examining the association between serum osteocalcin and
measures of liver steatosis do not differentiate between the total and uncarboxylated
forms of osteocalcin, nor do they measure the other bone turnover markers. In the
current study, we measured total and uncarboxylated osteocalcin as well as other bone
turnover markers (β-CTx and PINP) in a liver biopsy cohort, and both of total and
uncarboxylated osteocalcin showed inverse correlation with liver steatosis,
inflammation, ballooning and fibrosis grades. Uncarboxylated osteocalcin had no
stronger correlation with liver steatosis than the total osteocalcin. Other bone turnover
markers had no significant association with liver histological steatosis, which
distinguished osteocalcin as a measure of bone turnover from its effect on liver lipid
metabolism. Different from most species, up to 50% of serum osteocalcin in humans is
undercarboxylated/uncarboxylated [43]. Thus, the measures of total osteocalcin may
reflect the level of active uncarboxylated osteocalcin, and significantly correlate with
human liver steatosis. Despite serum osteocalcin level was negatively correlated with
liver steatosis and fibrosis in both male and female participants in the first population
study, the effect of osteocalcin on the incidence and remission of NAFLD showed a sex

difference. Higher circulating osteocalcin level was associated with a lower incidence
and a higher remission rate of NAFLD solely in the female but not male participants
from Shanghai Changfeng Study. Similar sex-specific association between osteocalcin
and NAFLD was also observed in other human studies [23,28,29]. In fact, the sex
difference in the associations of circulating osteocalcin with type 2 diabetes [44], body
fat distribution [45] and skeletal muscle mass [46] has been reported previously. Since
testosterone can compete with osteocalcin to bind the receptor of osteocalcin——
GPRC6A [47], the high circulating free testosterone levels in male participants might be
responsible for the dissociation between osteocalcin and NAFLD found in our current
study.
Osteocalcin was reported to increase energy expenditure, promote insulin
secretion and improve insulin sensitivity [13], which could improve liver steatosis and
glucose metabolism through multiple metabolic benefits, as observed in 3-week
osteocalcin treated mice in our current study. Two recent studies with osteocalcin
knock-out mouse model showed no metabolic dysfunction for unknown reason [14,15],
which are contrary to other studies and our current report. One possible explanation is
that the germ line knockout of the protein might induce a compensatory mechanism in
early age of these animals, which restored the lipid and carbohydrate metabolism to
control mice. Another two recent studies indicated that osteocalcin alleviated hepatic fat
accumulation through either improved glucose metabolism or ameliorated lipid
absorption [25, 26]. In our mouse model, we found that uncarboxylated osteocalcin
might have direct effect on liver lipogenesis pathway. With a short period of osteocalcin
treatment, hepatic lipogenic gene and protein expression was dramatically reduced,

without changing of glucose metabolism or insulin sensitivity. Overexpression of
SREBP-1c at a stable level could completely abolish the effect of osteocalcin on hepatic
lipogenesis pathway and circulating triglycerides. Taken together, osteocalcin could
directly target at liver lipogenesis pathway and inhibit the expression of hepatic SREBP-
1 and its downstream de novo lipogenesis proteins.
Circulating osteocalcin was also inversely associated with liver enzymes,
histological inflammation and fibrosis grades, and NAFLD fibrosis score in our current
study. A previous Spanish study of 69 NAFLD patients indicated lower osteocalcin was
correlated with severer liver fibrosis [27]. Several experimental studies indicated that
exogenous osteocalcin could alleviate liver inflammation and oxidative stress [31,48],
and protected against NASH in mouse models [48]. The mechanism underlying the
effect of osteocalcin on liver inflammation and fibrosis still requires further investigation.
Our results indicated that osteocalcin might be used as one of the blood
biomarkers to predict personal NAFLD risk and outcomes at least in female adults.
Female adults with serum osteocalcin below 25th percentile of the whole population had
90% higher risk of incident NAFLD, and NAFLD patients with serum osteocalcin below
25th percentile of the whole population had about 44% lower chance to achieve
remission of NAFLD. A direct effect of exogenous synthetic human decarboxylated
osteocalcin in reducing hepatic de novo lipogenesis via reducing the expression of
SREBP-1c was also detected in both male and female mouse models, which might be
promising to treat NAFLD in human beings.
Several limitations are associated with our current study. First, the histological
information for liver steatosis and fibrosis was not available for the large-scale

prospective cohort from the Shanghai Changfeng Study, and we used a noninvasive
ultrasound quantitative method for LFC to reflect liver steatosis grades and a NAFLD
fibrosis score (NFS) to estimate liver fibrosis grades. The LFC measured by the
ultrasound quantitative method is highly consistent with LFC measured by 1H-MRS
(r=0.89, P<0.001) [37] and histological liver steatosis grades (r=0.79, P<0.001) [49]
according to previous studies from our and other groups. The sensitivity and specificity
of NFS is problematic compared with histologically confirmed fibrosis score, and the
association between osteocalcin and liver fibrosis evaluated by NFS found in our
community cohort should be interpreted with caution. Second, the active form of
osteocalcin, uncarboxylated osteocalcin, was not assessed in the Shanghai Changfeng
Community cohort. However, we have demonstrated that serum uncarboxylated
osteocalcin was highly correlated with total osteocalcin, and showed similar correlation
with NAFLD in comparison with total osteocalcin in the liver biopsy cohort. Thus, the
serum total osteocalcin might be able to reflect the variation of serum uncarboxylated
osteocalcin and its correlation with NAFLD in the large-scale general population. Third,
this study was performed in two Chinese adult cohorts, and the results need to be
further evaluated in participants from different ethnicities.
Conclusion
Circulating osteocalcin was inversely associated with liver steatosis and fibrosis grades,
and could potentially help predicting the incidence and outcome of NAFLD in the female
population. Exogenous supplement of uncarboxylated osteocalcin could alleviate liver
steatosis and reduce hepatic lipogenesis via inhibiting SREBP-1c expression, which
might serve as a potential treatment of NAFLD.
